translations.text: Ptolemy Philometor had learned from those who returned to him that Antiochus had seized the territories over which he had ruled and taken them from him. He ordered all his forces, cavalry and infantry alike, to arm themselves. He also took his sister Arsinoe with him and came to the region of Raphia, where Antiochus’s army was encamped.

A man named Theodotus, wishing to carry out his plot, devised a plan and took with him armed warriors from Ptolemy’s forces who had previously pledged themselves to him. He came at night and attacked Ptolemy’s tent, intending to kill him alone and thus bring [?] to an end.

But Dositheus son of Drimylus, who was called a Jew and had subsequently accepted the Law, though he was a stranger to the covenant of the ancestors, learned of this. He placed a poor man in Ptolemy’s tent, and that man happened to be killed in the king’s place.

A fierce battle took place, and matters were going very well for Antiochus. But Arsinoe went among the troops with her hair loose, weeping with many tears and sobs. She begged them to save themselves, their wives, and their children and to fight bravely. She promised to give each of them two minas of gold if they fought and won.
And so it happened: all their opponents fell before them, and they captured many of them wounded.
After Ptolemy had won, he decided to go up to the nearby cities and rebuild them.
He did this, granted exemptions to the temples of their religion, and gave them gifts. He strengthened them and established them under his authority.

The Jews also sent some of the elders and leaders of the people to Philometor to greet him and bring him a gift and congratulations on his victory. When he received these from them, he was pleased and became all the more eager to visit them.
He came to Jerusalem and offered sacrifices to the great and mighty God. He also honored the place with many offerings.
For when he saw the buildings of the place, its orderly arrangement, and the splendor of the temple, he decided to enter the temple’s interior as well.

But they told him, “You are not permitted to do this, because neither the members of our people nor even all the priests are permitted to enter, but only the high priest, once a year.” Yet he was not persuaded by any of this.
They brought the Law and read it before him, but he still would not be persuaded. Instead, he said, “I must enter. Even if they have been deprived of this honor, I will not be deprived of it.”
He kept questioning them, saying, “How is it that, when I enter all the temples of worship, none of those inside them has stopped me?”
One of them answered him confidently, "You are wickedly [?] this."
But he answered, "Whether you wish it or not, I must enter."

The priests put on their sacred garments and fell facedown, crying out and pleading before the great and mighty God to help and rescue them and to turn aside the king’s evil intention and wicked plan. They filled the temple with tears and the sound of crying.
All the inhabitants of the city, trembling and alarmed, rushed out and waited to see what would happen.
The young women who had been kept secluded came out with their mothers, with dust and ashes on their heads. They went about the streets with weeping, tears, and sobs.
Brides who had just married left their bridal chambers for the moment, abandoning the covering that marked their modesty, and ran about bewildered in the street without shame.
Women left their babies and wandered here and there through the streets and open places. All the people gathered and came to the glorious temple.
They cried out and pleaded that his intention and everything he had planned might be thwarted.
When the people saw that he was insisting on entering and could not be persuaded to abandon his evil intention,

They called loudly to one another to take up their weapons and be ready to die bravely for the Law and the covenants of their ancestors. There was great uproar and turmoil in the place. With difficulty, some of the priests and elders stood up, forcibly restrained the people, and turned them to prayer and cries for help.
All the people stood before them in prayer and supplication.
The officials and dignitaries who were with the king tried every means, begging and urging him to turn back and abandon his evil intention and wicked plan.
But he was not persuaded by any of this. Instead, he grew proud and arrogant and began to enter by force, thinking he would carry out his intention.

While these things were happening, even those who were with him saw what was happening and turned back in fear. They saw all our people pleading and calling upon the one who holds authority over everything to bring retribution and disaster upon their enemies, and not to turn his gaze away from the wicked deed and the act of arrogance and pride being committed in violation of the Law.
They all gathered together, pleading and crying out with sobs beyond description.

For the sound was such that it seemed that not only human beings were crying out, but also the walls and foundations, and even the earth itself. All of them were surrendering their lives to death for the sake of the temple, so that it would not be defiled.
Then Simon the high priest knelt before the altar, stretched out his hands, and prayed wisely, saying:

Lord, Lord, King of heaven and Master of all, holy Judge, who alone is foremost among the holy ones, ruler of all, look upon us! See, we are being oppressed by one who is unclean, defiled, and arrogant, and by a weak and wretched force.
For you are the one who created everything, and you uphold everything by your righteous power. For you are the one who makes all those who exalt and uplift themselves [?].

You judged the people of old who committed injustice, including the giants who were with them, who trusted in the strength of their might. You destroyed them with the vast, unstoppable waters of the flood.

You burned the people of Sodom with fire and sulfur when their wickedness was revealed and became known, because they were proud and exalted themselves in their deeds. You made them an astonishing spectacle to all the generations after them.

You punished and scourged the great and arrogant Pharaoh, who enslaved your holy people Israel, with every kind of plague. You made known the power of your greatness and displayed your mighty dominion.

When he pursued your people with horses, chariots, and a great multitude, you drowned him in the depths of the sea with his entire army. But those who trusted in you, believing that you can do whatever you wish throughout all creation, you kept safe and sound.
And when your servants saw, they praised you, Almighty.

You, the King who made the earth, which cannot be measured or surveyed, chose this city and sanctified this place for your name, which needs nothing. You glorified it by revealing the greatness of your splendor, and you gave it a name and a covenant for the praise of your great and honored name.

Because you established and loved the house belonging to the people of Israel, you promised them that if they sinned and turned away from you, and afflictions and troubles overtook them, and they came and prayed in this place, you would hear their plea.
And now, you are faithful and true.
For on the many occasions when our ancestors were oppressed, you helped them out of their afflictions and rescued them from every trouble and every danger.
And now, holy King, because of our great and numerous sins, see, we are being oppressed and subjected to our enemies, and we remain in our weakness.
See, this wicked, unclean, and defiled man wishes to dishonor the holy place that was chosen and made known on earth for your excellent and holy name.
For your dwelling is in the highest heaven, exalted above all human beings.
But because you wished your glory to dwell among your people Israel, you consecrated this place.

Therefore, do not exact punishment from us through the uncleanness of these people, or rebuke us through their defilement, so that the unjust may not boast in their wickedness or rejoice in their arrogant speech and say:
‘We have trampled the sanctuary just as the temples of idols are trampled.’
But wipe away our sins, forgive our offenses, and let your face shine upon us at this hour.
Let your mercy come quickly to meet us, Lord. Put your praise in the mouths of the humble and the brokenhearted, and grant us peace.

But in this place the Lord God, who sees everything, the Father of fathers and the Holy One of holy ones, heard his prayer and plea, and scourged the man who only a little earlier had been boasting and exalting himself,

on every side, and tormented him with great distress. He collapsed and fell to the ground, trembling all over like a reed before the wind, so that he could not even speak a word because of the just judgment that had overtaken him.
When his friends and guards saw the severe punishment that had overtaken him, they were afraid that he might even die. Immediately they dragged him out, filled with great fear.
After a little while, however, he revived and came to his senses. He would not turn away from his stubborn purpose, but threatened them with great and fierce anger, then departed from there.
When Philometor went to Egypt, his wickedness continued to grow and increase, together with that of all his nobles and friends, who were devoid of all righteousness.

Their many, countless [?] did not satisfy him. Instead, he went so far in his insolence that he spoke blasphemous words against the place. Many of his friends, seeing the king's intention, also agreed with the wicked man's purpose.
The king wrote and issued a decree against our people. He made a carved image and set it up between the towers of the courtyard.

He wrote that anyone who did not sacrifice to it was not to enter the temple of God, and that all Jews were to be registered and brought into service and the subjection of slavery. Those among them who resisted were to be brought by force and killed by torture.
Those who were registered were to be branded with fire with the mark of Dionysus, so that they would be under the king's subjection.

So that it would not appear to many that we were coercing them by force, he wrote as follows: All those among them who wish to share in the beliefs of our religion are to be registered as Alexandrians, citizens of his city, the king's city.

A few of them, whose minds were not firmly established in the practice of reverence for God and in the ordinances of our city, readily gave themselves up to the king’s command, as though they were taking part in something good and excellent.

But the majority of the people took courage and stood heroically firm. They did not abandon or depart from any righteous practice, but surrendered their possessions in exchange for their lives, to save themselves from registration.

They hoped and waited for deliverance to come to them. Those who separated themselves and withdrew from them they regarded as unclean and considered enemies, excluding them from the privilege of fellowship in their assemblies.

As soon as the wicked man heard these things, he became very angry. He was furious not only with those living in Alexandria, but also became a fierce opponent of the people living throughout the country. He ordered that they all be gathered together quickly and urgently and put to a cruel and bitter death.

When this order was given, a malicious and bitter report about our entire people was spread by men who had turned away from the law, because they had not been allowed to share in fellowship with them.
The Jews, however, maintained their loyalty to the king.
They were careful to observe God’s ordinances and laws and maintained the distinctions between foods. Because of this, many regarded them as arrogant and conceited.
Yet they conducted themselves with justice in everything they did and were seen to be chosen and distinguished above all other people.
As for the decree issued against our people that they should be counted among the nations, they were unable to register them by force.

Because they would not give themselves over to the others’ foods and acts of worship, a report was spread against them that they were saying, “We neither respect the king nor consent to serve his forces.” They were described as rebellious people who strongly opposed the king’s commands and wishes. It was no casual matter when their enemies spread their hatred and malicious report.

The Gentiles living in the city had seen nothing wrong in the Jews who lived among them. They saw the calamity and turmoil that had suddenly overtaken them and the frantic rush of coercion, but could do nothing to help them, because the decree against them was harsh and severe. In great distress, however, they pleaded and appealed to their oppressors, saying to them:
“Do not afflict them so harshly! Surely this whole multitude of people cannot be destroyed when they have committed no offense.”

Some of their friends and neighbors also began buying them back from their captors. They sought to persuade the oppressors by a ruse, telling them, “We will make them offer sacrifices.” The Jews themselves, however, continued in prayer and cries for help, waiting and looking for deliverance to come to them.

But the king boasted, exalted himself, and grew arrogant in his unsettled mind. He paid no attention to the sovereignty of the great God, but supposed that he would always remain in this frame of mind and in this position of power. He wrote and sent the following letter against them:
“King Ptolemy Philometor, to the generals, governors, and soldiers of Egypt and every region: greetings and good health.
“I too am well, and our affairs [?].
“After we had won the victory and returned from the war we fought in Asia, which you yourselves also know about, with the help of the unconquerable gods who were with us,
“we wished to deal with all the peoples living in Syria and Phoenicia, not with oppression or force, but with great gentleness and mercy, as indeed we did.
“We gave many substantial offerings to all the priests in every city. We also decided to go to Jerusalem and honor the temple of those people who are always guilty and senseless.
“They welcomed our arrival in words, but in practice treated us as strangers. For when we wished to enter their temple and honor it with gifts and great honors,
“in the arrogance and conceit that possessed them, they prevented us from entering. They thus deprived themselves of the honor we wished to show them in keeping with our love for everyone.

“They openly displayed their hatred toward us, as though we ruled only over the other nations. In their arrogance and conceit, they treated those who had always been their benefactors with contempt and showed them no love at all.
“We were deeply distressed by these people’s insolence and lack of sense. We returned victoriously to Egypt and received all the peoples with joy and peace, acting as was fitting for us.

We had no resentment or anger against these people or their fellow countrymen, because we were living in equality and harmony. We entrusted affairs to them and left them in their hands. We forgave the offenses and insolent acts they had committed many times before, and we wished to register them as Alexandrians, citizens of our city and partners with the priests of our ancestors.
But they looked for and awaited hostility, and through the wickedness planted within them they rejected kindness and cast it away from themselves, because they always looked toward evil.

Not only did they fail to break free and turn away from their foolish and contemptible religion, but they also despise, in word and deed, those few among them whom they find to be loving and peaceful toward us. They continually oppose us and overturn every command and law laid down by us.
They oppose us in everything. And perhaps, if we should happen to go to war with our enemies, these wicked and guilty people will join them against us and become our betrayers and enemies.

For this reason, then, we have issued and sent this command: the very moment you receive this letter of ours, arrest those described in it, together with their wives, their children, and everything they possess. Send them to us in disgrace and imprisonment, bound in iron and subjected to every kind of hardship.
For when these people have been removed from among us and destroyed, we will always have peace and tranquility in our kingdom, and you will advance, prosper, and gain my favor.
But if anyone hides any of the Jews, from old people down to children and nursing infants, he shall die in suffering and many torments, together with his entire household.

Whoever comes forward and informs against him shall be given the property of the person found guilty of this offense, and shall receive three thousand pieces of silver from Caesar’s treasury, freedom, and a crown.
Every place where a Jew is found hiding shall be burned with fire and laid waste like a wilderness, and the people in it shall be wiped out and perish from among humankind.
Such was the wording of the copy of the letter.

Wherever this command was heard, there was joy, great rejoicing, and delight among the Gentiles, like people who had been waiting for this to happen and had now been openly given permission to carry it out.

But there was great mourning among the Jews. They wept aloud, cried out, and sighed deeply, for pain and sorrow had reached their very hearts. Distress surrounded them on every side, and a sentence of destruction and death had suddenly come upon them, which they had not expected.
For what city or inhabited place, what streets or open country, were not filled with mourning and great lamentation?

For they were being arrested by the governors in every city with violence and great, bitter oppression, and they were being tortured. Their suffering was so harsh and bitter that when their enemies saw it, they were grieved and wept over them.
For they saw many honored elders being led away in disgrace and with great violence, without anyone showing them even the slightest respect.

Brides who had only just married left the bridal chambers of their youth and took up weeping instead of joy. Instead of perfume, they poured ashes over their heads. They were brought along by force, stripped of their bridal veils and modesty.
They were shackled and bound in iron by foreign peoples, driven along in distress, and brought through the streets to the ships.

Their husbands, too, were driven along and brought by force. Instead of crowns, they wore iron collars around their necks. Instead of the joy and delight of youth and the rejoicing of the remaining days of their wedding feast, they were in mourning, weeping, and sighing, for they saw their death before their eyes.
They were forced down into the ships like animals, shackled and bound in iron. Some were bound by their necks and others by their feet.
Others were shackled and bound to the ships’ planks, so that they were hemmed in on every side in every possible way and had not even the slightest relief.

When they had all boarded the ships and come to the king, he ordered them to camp outside the city in a spacious place, exposed to disgrace and public humiliation, so that anyone who wished could go out and look at them. He surrounded and encircled them with a force of his soldiers so that none of them could escape.
After he had done this, he heard that some of their fellow countrymen were going out to them, weeping and sighing over the misery and calamity that had befallen their brothers.
He became furious and very angry, and ordered that these people too should be subjected to every torment, just like their companions, with nothing less inflicted on them than on the others.
He also ordered them all to be registered by name, and set a day on which he would destroy and wipe them all out.
They began registering them under harsh and bitter oppression, working with great diligence from sunrise until sunset. He had given them forty days to register them all.

Meanwhile, the king rejoiced and enjoyed himself, holding a great drinking feast in the temple of his idols, in the blindness and great arrogance that possessed him. With his defiled mouth and foolish mind, he praised blind, mute idols that neither spoke nor heard. He despised and rejected justice and righteousness, and spoke blasphemous words.
After the time appointed for the registrars, they approached the king and said to him, “We are unable to register all the Jews, because they are so numerous.
They cannot be counted, because the country is full of them, and there is no house without some of them in it. It is certain that the governors of Egypt cannot count them.”

When the king heard these things, he became very angry with them, claiming that they had taken bribes from the Jews and had seized on an excuse to say these things about them. Then they came forward and earnestly tried to convince him.
They showed him the sheets of papyrus on which they had registered them, and told him that they had also used up and exhausted all their writing reeds.
This happened through the working of God’s invincible power to help the Jews.

Then the king summoned Hermon, who had been appointed chief and overseer of the elephants, and ordered him to take great care of the elephants, for he was raging and filled with uncontrollable anger and fury.

He said to him, “Tomorrow give all the elephants, numbering about five hundred, plenty of frankincense and undiluted wine to drink. Drive them mad with a great quantity of intoxicating drink, so that he may come and unleash them against the Jews to destroy and annihilate them.”
After giving these orders, he turned to his pleasures and summoned his friends and his officials, those who hated the Jews most intensely.
The supervisor of the elephants, whose name was Arharot, carried out what had been commanded to Hermon.

Their servants went out every evening and bound the hands of the wretched and poor people. They watched them and guarded them with the utmost vigilance, expecting and awaiting the complete destruction of them all in the morning.
But the Jews, who seemed to the nations to have no help, not even a little, from anywhere, because of their chains and bitter afflictions,
cried out, pleaded, and prayed without ceasing before God, the ruler of all and Lord of all powers, the merciful God and Father, with sobbing and many tears,
that he would save them from the evil intention and plan being devised against them, openly display his salvation among them, and rescue them from the bitter death prepared for them.
Their plea for these things rose continually.
Hermon gave the merciless elephants wine mixed with frankincense to drink and made them drunk. At daybreak he came to the king’s courtyard to inform him of this.
But the Merciful One, the King of kings, cast sleep upon the king.

But the king slept in a deep sleep from evening until the ninth hour, through the action of him who rules over all. He was delayed far beyond the time appointed for destroying them, and his proud and arrogant purpose was thwarted.

When the Jews saw that they had escaped the hour appointed for them, they gave thanks and praised their holy God. Again they pleaded and begged the Merciful One to be fully reconciled to them and to show and make known the strength and help of his arm among the proud and arrogant nations.
For when it was nearly the tenth hour, his chief steward saw that all those invited by the king had arrived for the meal. He approached the king and nudged him in the side.
He woke with difficulty, and the steward informed him that it was time for the meal and told him about everything that the king himself had planned to do.
When he heard this, he went to the drinking feast and ordered all who had come for their meal to recline opposite him.
He encouraged them to enjoy themselves, and when evening came, they lingered long over their drinking.
With a torrent of words and fierce anger, the king summoned Hermon and questioned him about why the Jews had escaped the day appointed for their destruction.
He answered him, “I prepared and made ready everything you commanded during the night.” His friends also testified and said that he had done so.

When the king heard this, he did not humble himself or abandon his proud and arrogant purpose. Instead, he spoke defiantly and said to them, “They have sleep to thank for today. But tomorrow, without delay, make ready everything you were ordered to do, and prepare the elephants for the destruction and annihilation of the Jews.”
When the king had given these orders, all his nobles went home rejoicing.
Sleep did not come to them because of their anxious concern and their scheming about how to destroy and annihilate the Jews.
When the rooster crowed and dawn was near, Hermon equipped the elephants and came before the king’s courtyard.
The whole city was gathering to witness the injustice that was prepared to befall the Jews at daybreak.

When the Jews saw that the appointed hour for their destruction was approaching, they wept with many tears, stretched out their hands toward heaven, and cried out, asking the great and mighty God to help them quickly and urgently.
The king rose before sunrise and waited for his friends. Hermon approached and brought all the elephants past him, equipped and armed as the king had commanded.

When he saw them, he was amazed and astonished at the preparations for this wickedness. His thinking was completely blinded, and he asked them whether everything he had commanded had been carefully carried out.
This was God's providence: he had put forgetfulness into the king's heart concerning what he had previously been planning.
Hermon and all his friends approached and said to the king, “Everything you commanded is prepared and ready, both the elephants and the troops.”

When he heard these things from them, he was filled with great anger. For God's friends had desired [?], and he had frustrated his entire plan. He looked sternly at Hermon, insulted him with harsh words, and said to him:

“If they were your own people and members of your family, would you so mercilessly give the elephants drink and make them drunk, as you have done against the Jews, my friends and loved ones, who are faithful in everything?”
Were it not for our great mercy toward everyone, I would have destroyed your life in their place.”
Hermon was so terrified that he was only a little way from death. His color changed, and he was humbled from his proud attitude.
When the king's friends saw this, they too drew back in great fear and dismissed the people who were with them, each to his own place and work.
When the Jews heard the king's words, they praised and thanked the Lord God, the King of kings, who had turned toward them and become their helper.
When the king had finished with these matters, he and all his friends went to the banquet.
He summoned Hermon and said to him angrily, “How often must someone give you orders concerning these wretches?
Go, prepare the elephants and make them ready for tomorrow, for the destruction and ruin of the Jews.”
But his friends and relatives who were reclining with him saw his confused mind and unstable thinking, and said to him:
“King, how long will you keep testing us? Look, you have commanded their destruction three times, and then you turn around and cancel your commands.”
Because of this, the city too is gathering in crowds and is close to being entirely ruined by the daily turmoil.”

When the king heard this, he was filled with pride and arrogance. His entire understanding was blinded, and he forgot the help the Jews had received before and how his plan had already been frustrated three times. He swore an oath that would not be fulfilled, saying, “Tomorrow, before anything else, I will send these people to Sheol, parents and children together, furiously crushing them and trampling them underfoot.

Then I will march against Judea again and quickly crush it, destroy it with sword and fire, and make it like a plain. Their temple, which they prevented me from entering, I will quickly burn with fire. The place where they offer sacrifices I will lay waste and make a wilderness forever.”

Then his friends and relatives left him joyfully, having heard him confirm with an oath that he would destroy them. They went and made preparations, assembling troops in the city's open spaces to keep watch over the Jews.
The man in charge of the elephants gave them drink and made them drunk, as he had been commanded. He greatly excited them with wine and frankincense and brought them to an open space in the city.
A great crowd had gathered outside the city to watch the wicked spectacle. The man in charge of the elephants entered the king's courtyard and reported to him, inflaming his mind.

When the king heard this, he was filled with fury, great anger, and wicked thoughts. He took his entire army, along with the elephants and all his equipment, and went out. With a hard heart and an evil eye, he wanted to look on and see the death and suffering of the poor and unfortunate.
When the elephants went out through the city gate, a great crowd followed them. When the Jews saw the great cloud of dust rising and heard the mighty noise of the commotion,

they thought that the hour of their final end had come. Weeping and shedding many tears, they kissed one another, and each embraced his relatives. Others looked at the nursing infants and wept and sighed over them, because the hour of their end had arrived.
Then they remembered the help and deliverance from heaven that they had received in the past. They all threw themselves to the ground and took the infants from their mothers' breasts.
With sobbing and a loud, mighty cry, they called to the one whose power can accomplish whatever he wills, asking him in his great mercy to help those who now stood at the gates of death.

Eleazar, a well-known man who was one of the priests of the firstborn, was advanced in years and faultless in every aspect of his service to God. He instructed the elders with him to pray and plead with the holy God. He too prayed, saying:
“King, mighty in dominion, Most High, who rules over all and governs your entire creation with mercy,

Look and turn toward Abraham’s descendants and the children of Jacob, your holy one—the holy portion you chose for yourself, your people in a foreign land, a displaced and poor people who are perishing without cause through injustice, Father.

You drowned and destroyed Pharaoh, the mighty ruler of Egypt, in the depths of the sea, together with his strong and lofty army. He had multiplied his chariots and exalted himself, puffed up with great arrogance and a tongue that spoke boastfully. But you made the light of mercy shine upon Israel’s descendants.

You crushed and humbled Sennacherib, king of Assyria, Lord. He had exalted himself and boasted about his countless army, which had conquered and seized many lands. He even exalted himself against your holy city and spoke words of blasphemy and arrogance. You made your great and mighty dominion known to many nations.

You preserved the three companions in Babylon, who surrendered themselves to burning fire rather than serve worthless and empty things. You kept them safe inside the fiery furnace and brought them out whole, without even a hair being harmed, while the flame of fire burned their enemies.
You also brought Daniel out into the light unharmed, after he had been slandered and lowered into the lions’ den for them to maul and destroy him.

And Jonah was thrown into the depths of the sea and swallowed by a fish. He wept and prayed before you from the fish’s belly, and you heard his voice, kept him alive, and delivered him from the fish’s belly. You showed your power and greatness to all generations, Father.

And now, as we suffer humiliation and great distress, you, the merciful one who spreads your wings over everyone, look and turn quickly toward Israel’s descendants, for they are being humiliated by wicked and unclean nations.
If our sins and offenses testify against us that we should die in this way, rescue us, Lord, from the hands of our enemies, and discipline and destroy us yourself, with your own hand, as you wish.
Do not let the senseless praise their worthless gods for the destruction of your beloved people and say, ‘Even their God could not help them or rescue them.’

You are the Lord from whom all power and strength come, the same one from eternity. Now look, Lord, and have mercy on us, on those who are perishing without cause at the hands of unjust and senseless people.
Instead, let your unconquerable power be revealed today, so that it may bring fear and trembling upon these nations, tear their hearts apart, and rescue Israel’s descendants.
For a multitude of children and their people are pleading with you and begging you with tears and much weeping.

Let all the nations know that you are with us, Lord, and have not turned your face away from us. Just as you said, ‘Even when they were in the land of their enemies, I did not turn my eyes away from them,’ so now, Lord, fulfill this for us.
When Eleazar finished his prayer, the king came with his entire army and the equipment he had with him to the place where the Jews were staying.
When the Jews saw him, they cried out loudly to heaven, so that the whole earth shook and all the king’s forces were terrified by the sound of their cry.

Then the Lord, the Almighty, great in glory and the God of truth, made his holy face shine and opened the gates of heaven. Two glorious and fearsome angels descended, visible to no one except the Jews alone.
They stood facing the enemies and filled their entire army and their camps with fear, trembling, and terror. They bound and fettered them so that they could not move.
They brought trembling and shaking upon the king’s body, and he lost all his reason—that proud and arrogant man who had been blazing with anger and fury.
The elephants turned against his forces and trampled, destroyed, and killed them.
The king’s anger turned to compassion, and he wept over everything he had devised and prepared to do.
For when he heard the sound of their cry and saw them all lying facedown as though facing destruction, he wept, became furious with his friends, and said to them:

‘Your wickedness has surpassed that of kings and tyrants! You are scheming against your own benefactor, seeking how to take his authority away from him. Look, you see that my spirit is exhausted, yet you devise things that are harmful to the kingdom.
Who bound like this and brought here like animals those who maintained friendship with us and guarded the fortresses of our land?

Or who bound like this and subjected to harsh suffering those who have always, from the beginning, lived at peace with us, maintained friendship with us more than all the other nations, and often stood against our enemies?
Undo, undo these unjust bonds, and send them home in peace, for we plotted wickedly and brought them here.

Release the children of the Almighty, the God of heaven, who has long been with our ancestors and with us ourselves, who has preserved our kingdom from every crushing blow and distress and has always made our paths secure.’
When the king said these things, they were all released, and they blessed and thanked God their Savior because they had been rescued from death.

After this, the king entered the city and ordered that wine and provisions be given to the Jews for seven days. He said that in the very place where it had been arranged for them to die and perish, they should feast and rejoice over their deliverance.

Then those who had previously been insulted and had come close to death—indeed, had even reached it—celebrated their deliverance with joy instead of distress and bitter mourning. They divided up the place that had been prepared for them to fall and be buried in, making room for dining couches, and it was filled with feasting and gladness.

They put aside distress and mourning and took up the praises and psalms of their ancestors. With loud voices and shouting, they thanked and blessed God, who had performed wonders for them. They were glad and rejoiced over the sign of peace he had given them.
The king himself also held a great feast and invited a large crowd. He continually thanked the God of heaven, who had brought him deliverance with great glory.

But those who had previously prepared for the destruction of the Jews, and had joyfully registered their number so that they would become food for wild animals and birds, sighed and became distressed when they saw what was happening to them. They were covered with shame. Their insolence and their anger, which had burned like fire, were extinguished, and they were left in shame and disgrace.
The Jews, however, as we have already said, celebrated with feasting, rejoicing, and gladness, with psalms, praises, and thanksgiving.

They agreed among themselves that wherever they lived, they would observe these days with rejoicing and gladness, not for the sake of food and drink, but because of the deliverance God had brought them.
They approached the king and asked to be released and allowed to go home.
They had registered them from the twenty-fifth of the month until the fourth, forty days. For they had appointed three days for their destruction, from the fifth until the seventh.
During those days the Lord, who rules over all, revealed the glory of his greatness and his mercy, and saved them through a great wonder.
They all enjoyed what the king had given them until the fourteenth, when they approached the king to ask to be sent away.
The king praised them and wrote the following letter on their behalf to the governors in all the cities, expressing his great gratitude to them.
King Ptolemy Philometor, to all the governors in Egypt and to all those appointed over our affairs: peace and good health.
We ourselves and our children are well, and our affairs are prospering, because the great God has put our affairs in order as we wished.

Some of our friends and those who were very close to us, because of their hatred of the Jews, persuaded us to gather all the Jews under our authority, torture and destroy them, and torment them with every kind of suffering.
They said that the Jews would not allow our kingdom to enjoy peace and tranquility. They said this because of the hostility they bore toward all the Jews and the hatred they had for them.

They bound them and brought them here as though they were wicked, condemned men, without a trial or an investigation. They wanted to kill and destroy them all together, displaying wickedness, rage, and cruelty greater than that of the Scythians.

We were grieved by these things and became very angry. In keeping with the compassion and gentleness we show toward everyone, we barely managed to rescue them from death and spare their lives. We learned with certainty that God is the helper of the Jews and that, like a father fighting for his children, he fights on their behalf.
Considering their friendship and peaceful relations with us and our ancestors, we have left them free from every obligation.
We have ordered that whatever was taken from each of them be returned to him, and that no one wrong them even in the slightest or insult them over anything that has happened to them.

You must know that if we act deceitfully and do them any harm, or distress them in any way, we are acting not against human beings but against the Most High God, who rules over every power. For he is their avenger, and no one can flee or escape from him. Farewell.
When they received the letter, they did not wish to leave immediately. Instead, they asked the king that those Jews who had willingly turned aside and departed from the holy God and his law,
because of the greed of their bellies, should receive the punishment and judgment they deserved, since they had not been found faithful even in the king’s affairs.

When he heard that they were speaking truthfully, he accepted what they said, praised them, and gave them authority to kill and destroy all the apostates and lawbreakers under the rule of his kingdom, wherever they wished, at their own discretion.
Then the priests and the people praised the king as was fitting, raised their voices in praise to acclaim him, and went out rejoicing.
As they traveled along the road, they put every apostate who fell into their hands to a cruel and public death.
On that day they killed three hundred men, celebrated with feasting and great joy, and killed all those who had defiled themselves.

These people, for whom God had been a helper even in the face of death and whom he had completely rescued from every affliction, left the city crowned with all kinds of fragrant flowers. With joy and gladness they gave thanks and praised the God of their ancestors with great songs of praise, for he is forever the Savior of Israel.

When they came to Ptolemais, which is called Rose-Crowned because of the beauty of its setting, all the city's inhabitants came out together and welcomed them peacefully. They stayed there seven days.
They enjoyed themselves greatly, for the king had ordered that they be supplied with provisions at his expense until each one of them had gone home in peace.
They spent these days offering fitting praises and thanksgivings, and there too they established that they would celebrate those days with joy and gladness throughout their lives.

At the place where they had stayed, they set up a pillar and established a house of prayer. They departed joyfully, rejoicing and celebrating, each to his own region and city, by sea, by land, and by the rivers.
By the king’s command, they were exalted and raised above their enemies.
They recovered everything that had been plundered from them, and no one dared to wrong them even slightly, because of the great deliverance that the great and mighty God had brought about for them.
And blessed is the Savior of Israel forever and ever.
